His saying: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ means he contracted his face and turned away.

It is also read ʿabbasa with the doubled letter (tashdid).

﴿Because the blind man came to him﴾ is a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose): that is, "because the blind man came to him." The governing verb for it is either ʿabasa or tawalla, according to the disagreement between the Basrans and the Kufans over the question of tanazuʿ (competition between two verbs for one complement): which is preferred, giving effect to the first or to the second?

The exegetes have agreed that the occasion of revelation of the verse was: "Some nobles of Quraysh were with the Prophet ﷺ, and he had hoped for their conversion. Then ʿAbd Allah ibn Umm Maktum came, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked that Ibn Umm Maktum should cut off his speech, so he turned away from him, and this was revealed." The explanation of this will come, God willing, at the end of the discussion.

﴿And what could make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾: Glory be to Him turned to address His Prophet ﷺ, because direct address is more forceful in reproach. That is: what makes you aware of his state, so that you turn away from him? The clause ﴿perhaps he would purify himself﴾ is resumptive, to explain that he has a matter that is incompatible with turning away from him: that is, perhaps he would purify himself from sins through righteous deeds, due to what he learns from you. So the pronoun in "perhaps he" refers to the blind man. It has also been said that it refers to the disbeliever: that is, "And what could make you know that what you hoped for from those with whom you were occupied in speech, instead of the blind man, that they would purify themselves or be reminded?" The first is preferable.

The word of hope (tarajji) is in respect of the one addressed, to alert that turning away from him, while he is hoped to purify himself, is impermissible. The majority read ﴿Because the blind man came to him﴾ as a statement without interrogation, and its basis is what has preceded.

Al-Hasan read ʾan jaʾahu with the long vowel (madd) as an interrogative. On this reading it is connected to a deleted verb indicated by ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾, and the estimate is: "Did the blind man come to him, [that] he turned away and withdrew?" A parallel to this verse is His saying in Surat al-Anʿam: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and evening﴾ [al-Anʿam: 52]. Likewise His saying in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿And do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 28].

His saying: ﴿or he would remember﴾ is conjoined to "he would purify himself," included with it under the ruling of hope: that is, or he would remember and be admonished by what he has learned of the admonitions, ﴿so the reminder would benefit him﴾, i.e., the admonition.

The majority read "fa-tanfaʿuhu" with the nominative (raf'), while ʿAsim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa, al-Sulami and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read it with the accusative (nasb), as an answer to the optative/hope (jawab al-tarajji).

﴿As for the one who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾: that is, he was possessed of wealth and affluence, or he considered himself independent of faith and of what you possess of knowledge.

﴿you attend to him﴾: that is, you listen to his speech. Tasaddi means listening.

The majority read tasaddā with a single t (taxfif), by dropping one of the two tāʾs for lightness, while Nafiʿ and Ibn Muhaysin read it with doubling (tashdid), by assimilation (idgham). In this there is further repulsion for him ﷺ from turning towards them and listening to their speech.

﴿And it is not upon you that he does not purify himself﴾: that is, what is it upon you if he does not become Muslim and is not guided? For there is upon you only the conveying (of the message), so do not concern yourself with the affair of such disbelievers. It is permissible that "mā" be negating: that is, there is no harm upon you that the one to whom you turned and attended does not purify himself, and the clause is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "tasaddā."

Then Glory be to Him increased in reproaching His Messenger ﷺ, and said: ﴿But as for the one who came to you running﴾: that is, he reached you while being hasty in coming to you, seeking from you that you guide him to good and admonish him with the admonitions of Allah.

The clause ﴿while he fears﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "running" by interpenetration (tadakhkhul), or from the subject of "came to you" by coordination (tarādif).

﴿So you are unmindful of him﴾: that is, you are occupied away from him and turn away from attending to him, and talhhī means occupation and heedlessness. It is said: "lahaytu ʿan al-amr alhā," meaning I was occupied away from the matter; similarly "talahhaytu."

His saying: ﴿Nay [kallā]﴾ is a rebuke to him ﷺ concerning what he was reproached for: that is, do not do after this occurrence from you the like of it, of turning away from the poor and attending to the rich and being occupied with him, while he is not among those who purify themselves from receiving the guidance of what has come to you from the people of purification and acceptance of admonition. And this occurrence from the Prophet ﷺ is of the category of leaving the better course, so Allah, Glory be to Him, guided him to what is better for him.

﴿Indeed, it is a reminder﴾: that is, these verses or the surah are an admonition, whose due is that you be admonished by it, accept it, act upon its requirement, and that all your community act by it.

﴿So whoever wills, remembers it﴾: that is, whoever desires it is admonished by it, memorizes it and acts upon its requirement; and whoever turns away from it, as he did who considered himself self-sufficient, there is no need to concern oneself with his affair.

It has been said that the two pronouns in "innahā" and in "dhakarahu" refer to the Qur'an, and the feminine of the first is due to the feminine of its predicate.

It has been said that the first refers to the surah, or to the preceding verses.

The second refers to "tadhkirah" because it is in the sense of "dhikr."

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿whoever wills, remembers it﴾ is: whoever Allah wills, He inspires and makes him understand the Qur'an until he remembers it and is admonished by it; but the first is preferable.

Then Glory be to Him informed of the greatness and majesty of this reminder, and said: ﴿in scrolls﴾: that is, it is a reminder existing in scrolls. So the prepositional phrase is an attribute of "tadhkirah," and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. "Ṣuḥuf" is the plural of ṣaḥīfah. The meaning of ﴿honored﴾ is that it is honored with Allah because of the knowledge and wisdom in it, or because it descends from the Preserved Tablet. It has been said that by "ṣuḥuf" is meant the books of the prophets, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls, the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-Aʿla: 18–19].

The meaning of ﴿exalted﴾ is that it is high in rank with Allah. It has been said: exalted in the seventh heaven.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: ﴿honored﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet; ﴿exalted﴾, meaning in the seventh heaven.

Ibn Jarir said: exalted in rank and remembrance. It has also been said: exalted above resemblance and contradiction, purified, that is, sanctified, which none touch except the purified.

Al-Hasan said: purified from every defilement.

Al-Suddi said: protected from the disbelievers, who cannot reach it.

﴿In the hands of scribes﴾: "safarah" is the plural of "safir," like "katabah" and "katib." The meaning is that it is in the hands of scribes from among the angels, who copy the books from the Preserved Tablet.

Al-Farraʾ said: "The safarah here are the angels who carry the revelation between Allah and His Messenger, from al-sifārah, which is the mediation between people." He recited:

*"So I do not abandon mediation between my people, nor do I walk without a noble father."*

Al-Zajjaj said: The book was called "sifr" with a kasra on the sin, and the book is "sāfir," because its meaning is that it is clear. It is said: "asfara al-ṣubḥ" when it shines, and "asfarat al-mar'ah" when a woman uncovers her veil from her face; and from it: "safartu bayn al-qawm, usfiru sifārah," meaning I reconciled between them.

Mujahid said: they are the noble angels who record the deeds of the servants.

Qatadah said: the safarah here are the reciters, because they read the books.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they are the companions of the Prophet ﷺ.

Then Glory be to Him praised the safarah, and said: ﴿noble, obedient﴾ [karam, barara]: that is, noble with their Lord; thus said al-Kalbi.

Al-Hasan said: noble from sins, for they raise themselves above them.

It has been said: they are too noble to be with the son of Adam when he is alone with his wife or relieves his need.

It has been said: they prefer the benefits of others over their own benefits.

It has been said: they show nobility toward the believers by seeking forgiveness for them.

"Barara" is the plural of bārr, like kafarah and kāfir: that is, pious, obedient to their Lord, truthful in their faith; and its explanation has already preceded.

﴿Killed is man, how disbelieving he is!﴾: that is, cursed is the disbelieving man, how severe is his disbelief. It has been said: "destroyed" (ʿudhdhiba) is meant. It has been said that by the man is meant ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab. The meaning of ﴿how disbelieving he is!﴾ is amazement at the excess of his disbelief.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "Marvel, you, at his disbelief." It has been said that by "man" is meant the one previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿As for the one who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾. It has been said that it means the species, and this is the preferable view, so every intensely disbelieving disbeliever is included under it, and whoever was the cause of the revelation of the verse is included primarily.

Then Glory be to Him mentioned what this disbeliever should have considered, so that he might be restrained from his disbelief and refrain from his transgression. He said: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾: that is, from what thing did Allah create this disbeliever? The interrogative is for affirmation.

Then He explained that, saying: ﴿From a drop [nutfah] He created him﴾: that is, from a despised water, and this is belittling him.

Al-Hasan said: how can one who came out of the passage of urine twice be arrogant? The meaning of ﴿then He measured him﴾ is that He made him proportionate and prepared him for the interests of his self, and created for him the two hands, the two feet, the two eyes, and the rest of the instruments and senses. It has been said: He measured him in stages from one state to another: a drop, then a clot, until his creation was complete.

﴿Then the way He made easy for him﴾: that is, He made the path easy for him to good and evil.

Al-Suddi, Muqatil, ʿAta' and Qatadah said: He made it easy for him to come out from his mother's womb. The first is preferable.

Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. The accusative of "al-sabil" is by a hidden verb indicated by the mentioned verb: that is, He made the way easy, He made it easy for him.

﴿Then He causes him to die and buries him﴾: that is, He made him, after causing him to die, one having a grave in which he is concealed, honoring him, and did not make him one of those thrown upon the face of the earth to be eaten by beasts and birds. Thus said al-Farraʾ. Abu ʿUbaydah said: He made for him a grave and commanded that he be buried in it. He did not say "qabarahu," because the one who buries (qābir) is the one who interres with his own hand. From it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

*"If she had supported a dead man against her breast, he would have lived, and he would not have been moved to a gravedigger."*

﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him﴾: that is, then when He wills his resurrection, He raises him, that is, revives him after his death. He tied the resurrection to His will to indicate that its time is not fixed, but follows His will. The majority read "anshara-hu" with an alif; Abu Haywah narrated from Nafiʿ and Shuʿayb ibn Abi Hamzah "nashara-hu" without an alif, and both are eloquent dialects.

﴿Nay! He has not fulfilled what He commanded him﴾: "Nay" is a rebuke and deterrence for the disbelieving man: that is, the matter is not as he says.

The meaning of "lammā yaqḍi mā amarahu" is: he has not fulfilled what Allah commanded him, of acting in obedience and avoiding His disobediences. It has been said that the intended meaning is mankind in general, and that he did not do what Allah commanded him despite the long duration, because no one is free of shortcoming.

Al-Hasan said: that is, truly he did not act upon what he was commanded.

Ibn Fawrak said: that is, "Nay, he has not fulfilled for this disbeliever what He commanded him of faith; rather He commanded him with what he did not fulfill."

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping on "kallā" is ugly, and stopping on "amarahu" is good, and "kallā" by this is in the sense of "truly."

It has been said that the meaning is: not all individuals of mankind have fulfilled what He commanded, but some have neglected it: some through disbelief, and some through disobedience; and only a few have fulfilled what Allah commanded.

Then Glory be to Him began enumerating His blessings upon His servants so that they might be thankful and refrain from ingratitude, after mentioning the blessings connected with their coming into being. He said: ﴿So let man look at his food﴾: that is, let him look at how Allah created his food, which He made a cause of his life, and how He prepared for him the means of sustenance by which he prepares for eternal happiness. Mujahid said: its meaning is, "let man look at his food," that is, at its entry and its exit; but the first is preferable.

Then Glory be to Him explained that, saying: ﴿That We poured the water in torrents﴾. The majority read "innā" with a kasra, as a resumption. The Kufans and Ruways from Yaʿqub read it with a fatḥah, as a substitute (badal) from "his food," a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), since the descent of rain is a cause for the food's coming into being, so it is as though it includes it; or by estimating the lām of cause.

Al-Zajjaj said: the kasra is on the beginning and resumption, and the fatḥah is in the sense of a substitute from "food." The meaning: let man look at that We poured the water in torrents; and by pouring the water he meant the rain.

Al-Hasan ibn ʿAli read it with a fatḥah and imālah.

Then We split the earth, splitting it open [﴿ثُمَّ شَقَقْنا الأرْضَ شَقًّا﴾]: that is, We split it open with the vegetation that emerges from it due to the descent of rain, a wondrous splitting, with what comes forth from it in its smallness and greatness, its shape and its form.

Then He explained the cause of this splitting and what occurred for its sake, saying: ﴿فَأنْبَتْنا فِيها حَبًّا﴾ [So We caused grain to grow in it], meaning the grains on which one feeds. The meaning is that the plant continues to grow and increase until it becomes grain.

His statement ﴿وعِنَبًا﴾ [and grapes] is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ḥabban: that is, "and We caused grapes to grow in it." It has been said that it is not a requirement of conjunction that the conjoined element be restricted by all the restrictions that apply to the element it is conjoined to. So there is no harm in the growth of grapes being free of the splitting of the earth.

Al-qaḍb is the fresh fodder (qatt) that is cut again and again, and on which animals are fed. For this reason it is called qaḍb, as a verbal noun from qaḍaba-hu, meaning "he cut it," as if it is named for the repeated cutting of the same cut.

Al-Khalil said: al-qaḍb is fresh faṣfaṣa (alfalfa), and when it dries it becomes qatt.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: al-qaḍbah and al-qaḍb are the fresh (plant), and he said: the place where it grows is called muqaḍḍabah.

Al-Qutaybi and Tha'lab said: The people of Makkah call grapes al-qaḍb.

Al-zaytun is that from which oil is pressed, and it is the well-known olive tree. Al-nakhl is the plural of nakhlah (palm tree).

﴿وحَدائِقَ غُلْبًا﴾ [and dense gardens] is the plural of ḥadīqah, which is an orchard, and al-ghulb are the large ones, thick of neck.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: al-ghulb are those whose parts are intertwined with one another. It is said: rajul aghlab (a man with a thick neck) when he has a large neck, and the lion is called aghlab because its neck is solid and it does not turn except with its whole body.

Al-Ajjaj said:
"I kept twisting my back and my head on the day of parting,
until I became like the thick-necked one (al-aghlab)."

The plural of aghlab and ghalbā’ is ghulb, just as aḥmar and ḥamrā’ are pluralized as ḥumr.

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: al-ghulb are the noble palm trees.

It is also reported from Ibn Zayd and ʿIkrimah: they are thick at the middle and the trunks.

Al-fākihah is what a person eats of the fruits of trees, such as grapes, figs, peaches and the like.

Al-abb is everything the earth produces that people do not eat and do not cultivate, of herbage and all kinds of pasture. The poet's verse includes it:
"Our grandfather is Qays, and Najd is our home,
and for us there is al-abb therein, and the watering place."

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: al-abb is everything that grows on the face of the earth.

Ibn Abi Talhah said: it is the fresh fruits.

It is also reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he said: it is specifically figs, but the first (view) is more preferable.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to explain the conditions of the return (to Allah), saying: ﴿فَإذا جاءَتِ الصّاخَّةُ﴾ [So when the Deafening Blast comes], meaning the Blast of the Day of Resurrection. It is called al-ṣākhkhah because of the intensity of its sound, for it deafens the ears, that is, it makes them deaf so that they do not hear. It has been said that it is called ṣākhkhah because ears incline toward it, from the saying aṣāḫa ilā kadhā, meaning "he listened to it." The first is more correct.

Al-Khalil said: al-ṣākhkhah is a cry that deafens the ears until it renders them deaf through the severity of its impact. The root of the word in the language is derived from a violent striking; it is said ṣakhkhahu bil-ḥajar when he struck him with a stone.

The answer to (idhā) is omitted, indicated by His statement ﴿لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنهم يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ﴾ [for every man among them that day will have a matter that occupies him], meaning: when the Deafening Blast comes, each person will be preoccupied with himself.

The time expression in His statement ﴿يَوْمَ يَفِرُّ المَرْءُ مِن أخِيهِ﴾ [on the day a man flees from his brother] ﴿وأُمِّهِ وأبِيهِ﴾ [and his mother and his father] ﴿وصاحِبَتِهِ وبَنِيهِ﴾ [and his spouse and his children] is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿إذا جاءَتْ﴾ [when it comes], or is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning "I mean," and it serves as an explanation of al-ṣākhkhah, or it is a substitute for it and is indeclinable, built on fatḥah. He specified these people for mention because they are the closest of relatives, and their children are (the objects of) tenderness and compassion. So fleeing from them occurs only due to a great terror and a dreadful calamity.

﴿لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنهم يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ﴾: that is, every person on the Day of Resurrection has a matter that preoccupies him away from his relatives and turns him away from them.

It has been said that he flees from them out of fear of their demanding from him what is owed between them. It has been said that he flees from them so that they do not see what he is in of hardship. It has been said that it is because he knows they will not benefit him nor avail him anything, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُغْنِي مَوْلًى عَنْ مَوْلًى شَيْئًا﴾ [the day when no protecting friend will avail a protecting friend at all]. The sentence is resumptive (mustanafah), brought to explain the cause of the fleeing.

Ibn Qutaybah said: yughnīhi means "it turns him away from his relatives," and from it one says aghniʿannī wajhaka, meaning "turn your face away from me."

The majority recited yughnīhi with the ghayn dotted (ghayn mu‘jamah).

Ibn Muḥaysin recited it with the unpointed ʿayn with the yāʾ vowelled with fatḥah, meaning yuhimmuhu: from ʿanāhu al-amr when it concerned him (ahammahu).

﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُسْفِرَةٌ﴾ [Faces that Day will be bright], "wujūh" is the subject (mubtada’), although it is indefinite, because it is in a context of detailing, and this is one of the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun. "Yawma'idhin" is related to it, and "musfirah" is its predicate (khabar). The meaning of musfirah is radiant and shining, and these are the faces of the believers, because they know on that day what blessings and honor are theirs. One says asfara al-ṣubḥ when it shone.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: musfirah (bright) from the traces of wuḍūʾ (ablution). It has been said: from the standing in prayer at night.

﴿ضاحِكَةٌ مُسْتَبْشِرَةٌ﴾ [laughing, joyful], meaning rejoicing at what they attained of the immense reward.

Then, when He finished mentioning the condition of the believers, He mentioned the condition of the disbelievers, saying: ﴿ووُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْها غَبَرَةٌ﴾ [And faces that Day will be dust-covered], meaning dust and gloom because of what they see of the punishment Allah has prepared for them.

﴿تَرْهَقُها قَتَرَةٌ﴾ [darkness will cover them], meaning blackness and dimness will cover and overspread them. It has been said: humiliation. It has been said: severity. In the speech of the Arabs al-qatar is dust, so said Abu ʿUbaydah, and he recited the verse of al-Farazdaq:
"Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a host
over whom you see banners and dust (al-qatara)."

What Abu ʿUbaydah said is refuted by the earlier mention of al-ghabarah, for it is the singular of dust (ghubār).

Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-qatarah is what rises up to the sky, and al-ghabarah is what descends to the earth.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ [Those], meaning the owners of these faces, ﴿هُمُ الكَفَرَةُ الفَجَرَةُ﴾ [they are the disbelievers, the wicked], meaning those who combine disbelief in Allah with wickedness. One says fajara, meaning he transgressed; and fajara, meaning he lied. Its root is inclination, and the fājir is one who inclines away from the truth.

At-Tirmidhi, who graded it ḥasan, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, and Ibn Mardawayh, reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: "(The chapter) ʿAbasa wa tawallā was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktūm the blind man. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and began saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, guide me.' And with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was a man from the great leaders of the polytheists, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began turning away from him and turning toward the other, saying: 'Do you see any harm in what I say?' He would say, 'No.' So concerning this it was revealed."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, and Abū Yaʿlā reported from Anas, who said: "ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm came while he (the Prophet) was speaking with Ubayy ibn Khalaf, so he turned away from him, and Allah revealed ﴿عَبَسَ وتَوَلّى﴾ [He frowned and turned away] ﴿أنْ جاءَهُ الأعْمى﴾ [because the blind man came to him]. So after that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to honor him."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was conversing privately with ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, and he was greatly eager to confront them and was keen that they should believe, a blind man named ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm came toward them walking while he was speaking with them. ʿAbdullāh began asking the Prophet (ﷺ) to recite a verse of the Qur'an, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, teach me from what Allah has taught you.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away from him, frowned in his face, turned away, disliked his speech, and turned toward the others. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished his private conversation and began to return to his family, Allah took away part of his sight, then he nodded his head, and then Allah revealed ﴿عَبَسَ وتَوَلّى﴾ [He frowned and turned away], the verse. When what was revealed concerning him was revealed, the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) honored him, spoke to him, and said: 'What is your need? Do you want anything?' And when he went away from him, he would say: 'Do you have any need for anything?'" Ibn Kathīr said: "In it there is strangeness, and its chain has been criticized."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿بِأيْدِي سَفَرَةٍ﴾ [in the hands of scribes], that he said: "scribes."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from him regarding ﴿بِأيْدِي سَفَرَةٍ﴾ that he said: "They are, in Nabatean, the readers."

Ibn Jarīr also reported from him regarding ﴿كِرامٍ بَرَرَةٍ﴾ [noble and righteous], that he said: "The angels."

al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who recites the Qur'an and is proficient in it is with the noble, righteous scribes, and the one who recites it and finds it difficult has two rewards."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ﴾ [then He made the way easy for him], that he said: "He means by that his coming out from his mother's womb; He made it easy for him."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr regarding His statement ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرِ الإنْسانُ إلى طَعامِهِ﴾ [let man look at his food], that he said: "To its entrance and its exit."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرِ الإنْسانُ إلى طَعامِهِ﴾, that he said: "To his excrement."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him regarding ﴿أنّا صَبَبْنا الماءَ صَبًّا﴾ [that We poured down the water in torrents], that he said: "The rain." ﴿ثُمَّ شَقَقْنا الأرْضَ شَقًّا﴾: "From the vegetation."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim also reported from him regarding His statement ﴿وقَضْبًا﴾ [and fresh fodder], that he said: "The faṣfaṣah, meaning the qatt." ﴿وحَدائِقَ غُلْبًا﴾ [and dense gardens], he said: "Tall." ﴿وفاكِهَةً وأبًّا﴾ [and fruit and pasture], he said: "The fresh fruits."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim also reported from him, saying: "The ḥadā'iq are every densely intertwined (place), al-ghulb are what is thick, and al-abb is what the earth produces of what the animals eat and people do not eat."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also regarding ﴿وحَدائِقَ غُلْبًا﴾, that he said: "A tree in Paradise under which one takes shade, which bears nothing."

Ibn Jarīr reported from him also, saying: "Al-abb: the herbage and the pasture."

Abū ʿUbayd in his Faḍā'il and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Ibrahim al-Taymi, who said: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about al-abb, what is it? He said: "What sky would shade me and what earth would carry me if I say something in the Book of Allah that I do not know?"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn Yazīd that a man asked ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) about His statement ﴿وأبًّا﴾, and when he saw them saying (nothing), he turned toward them with the whip (al-durrah).

Ibn Saʿd, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab, and al-Khaṭīb reported from Anas that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) recited on the pulpit ﴿فَأنْبَتْنا فِيها﴾ [So We caused to grow therein] ﴿حَبًّا وعِنَبًا﴾ [grain and grapes], up to His statement ﴿وأبًّا﴾ [and pasture]. He said: "All of this we have known, so what is the abb?" Then he threw down a staff that was in his hand and said: "By the life of Allah, this is artificial (al-takalluf). What harm is there if you do not know what the abb is? Follow what has been made clear to you from this Book and act upon it, and what you do not know, leave it to its Lord."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Al-ṣākhkhah is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His statement, musfirah, that he said: "Radiant." And regarding His statement ﴿تَرْهَقُها قَتَرَةٌ﴾, he said: "Severity and humiliation cover them."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from him regarding qatarah, he said: "The blackness of the face."

Surah 80 (ʿAbasa) is Meccan, according to all scholars.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The surah of ʿAbasa was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ means he contracted his face and turned away.

It is also read ʿabbasa with the doubled letter (tashdid).

﴿Because the blind man came to him﴾ is a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose): that is, "because the blind man came to him." The governing verb for it is either ʿabasa or tawalla, according to the disagreement between the Basrans and the Kufans over the question of tanazuʿ (competition between two verbs for one complement): which is preferred, giving effect to the first or to the second?

The exegetes have agreed that the occasion of revelation of the verse was: "Some nobles of Quraysh were with the Prophet ﷺ, and he had hoped for their conversion. Then ʿAbd Allah ibn Umm Maktum came, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked that Ibn Umm Maktum should cut off his speech, so he turned away from him, and this was revealed." The explanation of this will come, God willing, at the end of the discussion.

﴿And what could make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾: Glory be to Him turned to address His Prophet ﷺ, because direct address is more forceful in reproach. That is: what makes you aware of his state, so that you turn away from him? The clause ﴿perhaps he would purify himself﴾ is resumptive, to explain that he has a matter that is incompatible with turning away from him: that is, perhaps he would purify himself from sins through righteous deeds, due to what he learns from you. So the pronoun in "perhaps he" refers to the blind man. It has also been said that it refers to the disbeliever: that is, "And what could make you know that what you hoped for from those with whom you were occupied in speech, instead of the blind man, that they would purify themselves or be reminded?" The first is preferable.

The word of hope (tarajji) is in respect of the one addressed, to alert that turning away from him, while he is hoped to purify himself, is impermissible. The majority read ﴿Because the blind man came to him﴾ as a statement without interrogation, and its basis is what has preceded.

Al-Hasan read ʾan jaʾahu with the long vowel (madd) as an interrogative. On this reading it is connected to a deleted verb indicated by ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾, and the estimate is: "Did the blind man come to him, [that] he turned away and withdrew?" A parallel to this verse is His saying in Surat al-Anʿam: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and evening﴾ [al-Anʿam: 52]. Likewise His saying in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿And do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 28].

His saying: ﴿or he would remember﴾ is conjoined to "he would purify himself," included with it under the ruling of hope: that is, or he would remember and be admonished by what he has learned of the admonitions, ﴿so the reminder would benefit him﴾, i.e., the admonition.

The majority read "fa-tanfaʿuhu" with the nominative (raf'), while ʿAsim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa, al-Sulami and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read it with the accusative (nasb), as an answer to the optative/hope (jawab al-tarajji).

﴿As for the one who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾: that is, he was possessed of wealth and affluence, or he considered himself independent of faith and of what you possess of knowledge.

﴿you attend to him﴾: that is, you listen to his speech. Tasaddi means listening.

The majority read tasaddā with a single t (taxfif), by dropping one of the two tāʾs for lightness, while Nafiʿ and Ibn Muhaysin read it with doubling (tashdid), by assimilation (idgham). In this there is further repulsion for him ﷺ from turning towards them and listening to their speech.

﴿And it is not upon you that he does not purify himself﴾: that is, what is it upon you if he does not become Muslim and is not guided? For there is upon you only the conveying (of the message), so do not concern yourself with the affair of such disbelievers. It is permissible that "mā" be negating: that is, there is no harm upon you that the one to whom you turned and attended does not purify himself, and the clause is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "tasaddā."

Then Glory be to Him increased in reproaching His Messenger ﷺ, and said: ﴿But as for the one who came to you running﴾: that is, he reached you while being hasty in coming to you, seeking from you that you guide him to good and admonish him with the admonitions of Allah.

The clause ﴿while he fears﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "running" by interpenetration (tadakhkhul), or from the subject of "came to you" by coordination (tarādif).

﴿So you are unmindful of him﴾: that is, you are occupied away from him and turn away from attending to him, and talhhī means occupation and heedlessness. It is said: "lahaytu ʿan al-amr alhā," meaning I was occupied away from the matter; similarly "talahhaytu."

His saying: ﴿Nay [kallā]﴾ is a rebuke to him ﷺ concerning what he was reproached for: that is, do not do after this occurrence from you the like of it, of turning away from the poor and attending to the rich and being occupied with him, while he is not among those who purify themselves from receiving the guidance of what has come to you from the people of purification and acceptance of admonition. And this occurrence from the Prophet ﷺ is of the category of leaving the better course, so Allah, Glory be to Him, guided him to what is better for him.

﴿Indeed, it is a reminder﴾: that is, these verses or the surah are an admonition, whose due is that you be admonished by it, accept it, act upon its requirement, and that all your community act by it.

﴿So whoever wills, remembers it﴾: that is, whoever desires it is admonished by it, memorizes it and acts upon its requirement; and whoever turns away from it, as he did who considered himself self-sufficient, there is no need to concern oneself with his affair.

It has been said that the two pronouns in "innahā" and in "dhakarahu" refer to the Qur'an, and the feminine of the first is due to the feminine of its predicate.

It has been said that the first refers to the surah, or to the preceding verses.

The second refers to "tadhkirah" because it is in the sense of "dhikr."

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿whoever wills, remembers it﴾ is: whoever Allah wills, He inspires and makes him understand the Qur'an until he remembers it and is admonished by it; but the first is preferable.

Then Glory be to Him informed of the greatness and majesty of this reminder, and said: ﴿in scrolls﴾: that is, it is a reminder existing in scrolls. So the prepositional phrase is an attribute of "tadhkirah," and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. "Ṣuḥuf" is the plural of ṣaḥīfah. The meaning of ﴿honored﴾ is that it is honored with Allah because of the knowledge and wisdom in it, or because it descends from the Preserved Tablet. It has been said that by "ṣuḥuf" is meant the books of the prophets, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls, the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-Aʿla: 18–19].

The meaning of ﴿exalted﴾ is that it is high in rank with Allah. It has been said: exalted in the seventh heaven.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: ﴿honored﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet; ﴿exalted﴾, meaning in the seventh heaven.

Ibn Jarir said: exalted in rank and remembrance. It has also been said: exalted above resemblance and contradiction, purified, that is, sanctified, which none touch except the purified.

Al-Hasan said: purified from every defilement.

Al-Suddi said: protected from the disbelievers, who cannot reach it.

﴿In the hands of scribes﴾: "safarah" is the plural of "safir," like "katabah" and "katib." The meaning is that it is in the hands of scribes from among the angels, who copy the books from the Preserved Tablet.

Al-Farraʾ said: "The safarah here are the angels who carry the revelation between Allah and His Messenger, from al-sifārah, which is the mediation between people." He recited:

*"So I do not abandon mediation between my people, nor do I walk without a noble father."*

Al-Zajjaj said: The book was called "sifr" with a kasra on the sin, and the book is "sāfir," because its meaning is that it is clear. It is said: "asfara al-ṣubḥ" when it shines, and "asfarat al-mar'ah" when a woman uncovers her veil from her face; and from it: "safartu bayn al-qawm, usfiru sifārah," meaning I reconciled between them.

Mujahid said: they are the noble angels who record the deeds of the servants.

Qatadah said: the safarah here are the reciters, because they read the books.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they are the companions of the Prophet ﷺ.

Then Glory be to Him praised the safarah, and said: ﴿noble, obedient﴾ [karam, barara]: that is, noble with their Lord; thus said al-Kalbi.

Al-Hasan said: noble from sins, for they raise themselves above them.

It has been said: they are too noble to be with the son of Adam when he is alone with his wife or relieves his need.

It has been said: they prefer the benefits of others over their own benefits.

It has been said: they show nobility toward the believers by seeking forgiveness for them.

"Barara" is the plural of bārr, like kafarah and kāfir: that is, pious, obedient to their Lord, truthful in their faith; and its explanation has already preceded.

﴿Killed is man, how disbelieving he is!﴾: that is, cursed is the disbelieving man, how severe is his disbelief. It has been said: "destroyed" (ʿudhdhiba) is meant. It has been said that by the man is meant ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab. The meaning of ﴿how disbelieving he is!﴾ is amazement at the excess of his disbelief.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "Marvel, you, at his disbelief." It has been said that by "man" is meant the one previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿As for the one who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾. It has been said that it means the species, and this is the preferable view, so every intensely disbelieving disbeliever is included under it, and whoever was the cause of the revelation of the verse is included primarily.

Then Glory be to Him mentioned what this disbeliever should have considered, so that he might be restrained from his disbelief and refrain from his transgression. He said: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾: that is, from what thing did Allah create this disbeliever? The interrogative is for affirmation.

Then He explained that, saying: ﴿From a drop [nutfah] He created him﴾: that is, from a despised water, and this is belittling him.

Al-Hasan said: how can one who came out of the passage of urine twice be arrogant? The meaning of ﴿then He measured him﴾ is that He made him proportionate and prepared him for the interests of his self, and created for him the two hands, the two feet, the two eyes, and the rest of the instruments and senses. It has been said: He measured him in stages from one state to another: a drop, then a clot, until his creation was complete.

﴿Then the way He made easy for him﴾: that is, He made the path easy for him to good and evil.

Al-Suddi, Muqatil, ʿAta' and Qatadah said: He made it easy for him to come out from his mother's womb. The first is preferable.

Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. The accusative of "al-sabil" is by a hidden verb indicated by the mentioned verb: that is, He made the way easy, He made it easy for him.

﴿Then He causes him to die and buries him﴾: that is, He made him, after causing him to die, one having a grave in which he is concealed, honoring him, and did not make him one of those thrown upon the face of the earth to be eaten by beasts and birds. Thus said al-Farraʾ. Abu ʿUbaydah said: He made for him a grave and commanded that he be buried in it. He did not say "qabarahu," because the one who buries (qābir) is the one who interres with his own hand. From it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

*"If she had supported a dead man against her breast, he would have lived, and he would not have been moved to a gravedigger."*

﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him﴾: that is, then when He wills his resurrection, He raises him, that is, revives him after his death. He tied the resurrection to His will to indicate that its time is not fixed, but follows His will. The majority read "anshara-hu" with an alif; Abu Haywah narrated from Nafiʿ and Shuʿayb ibn Abi Hamzah "nashara-hu" without an alif, and both are eloquent dialects.

﴿Nay! He has not fulfilled what He commanded him﴾: "Nay" is a rebuke and deterrence for the disbelieving man: that is, the matter is not as he says.

The meaning of "lammā yaqḍi mā amarahu" is: he has not fulfilled what Allah commanded him, of acting in obedience and avoiding His disobediences. It has been said that the intended meaning is mankind in general, and that he did not do what Allah commanded him despite the long duration, because no one is free of shortcoming.

Al-Hasan said: that is, truly he did not act upon what he was commanded.

Ibn Fawrak said: that is, "Nay, he has not fulfilled for this disbeliever what He commanded him of faith; rather He commanded him with what he did not fulfill."

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping on "kallā" is ugly, and stopping on "amarahu" is good, and "kallā" by this is in the sense of "truly."

It has been said that the meaning is: not all individuals of mankind have fulfilled what He commanded, but some have neglected it: some through disbelief, and some through disobedience; and only a few have fulfilled what Allah commanded.

Then Glory be to Him began enumerating His blessings upon His servants so that they might be thankful and refrain from ingratitude, after mentioning the blessings connected with their coming into being. He said: ﴿So let man look at his food﴾: that is, let him look at how Allah created his food, which He made a cause of his life, and how He prepared for him the means of sustenance by which he prepares for eternal happiness. Mujahid said: its meaning is, "let man look at his food," that is, at its entry and its exit; but the first is preferable.

Then Glory be to Him explained that, saying: ﴿That We poured the water in torrents﴾. The majority read "innā" with a kasra, as a resumption. The Kufans and Ruways from Yaʿqub read it with a fatḥah, as a substitute (badal) from "his food," a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), since the descent of rain is a cause for the food's coming into being, so it is as though it includes it; or by estimating the lām of cause.

Al-Zajjaj said: the kasra is on the beginning and resumption, and the fatḥah is in the sense of a substitute from "food." The meaning: let man look at that We poured the water in torrents; and by pouring the water he meant the rain.

Al-Hasan ibn ʿAli read it with a fatḥah and imālah.

Then We split the earth, splitting it open [﴿ثُمَّ شَقَقْنا الأرْضَ شَقًّا﴾]: that is, We split it open with the vegetation that emerges from it due to the descent of rain, a wondrous splitting, with what comes forth from it in its smallness and greatness, its shape and its form.

Then He explained the cause of this splitting and what occurred for its sake, saying: ﴿فَأنْبَتْنا فِيها حَبًّا﴾ [So We caused grain to grow in it], meaning the grains on which one feeds. The meaning is that the plant continues to grow and increase until it becomes grain.

His statement ﴿وعِنَبًا﴾ [and grapes] is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ḥabban: that is, "and We caused grapes to grow in it." It has been said that it is not a requirement of conjunction that the conjoined element be restricted by all the restrictions that apply to the element it is conjoined to. So there is no harm in the growth of grapes being free of the splitting of the earth.

Al-qaḍb is the fresh fodder (qatt) that is cut again and again, and on which animals are fed. For this reason it is called qaḍb, as a verbal noun from qaḍaba-hu, meaning "he cut it," as if it is named for the repeated cutting of the same cut.

Al-Khalil said: al-qaḍb is fresh faṣfaṣa (alfalfa), and when it dries it becomes qatt.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: al-qaḍbah and al-qaḍb are the fresh (plant), and he said: the place where it grows is called muqaḍḍabah.

Al-Qutaybi and Tha'lab said: The people of Makkah call grapes al-qaḍb.

Al-zaytun is that from which oil is pressed, and it is the well-known olive tree. Al-nakhl is the plural of nakhlah (palm tree).

﴿وحَدائِقَ غُلْبًا﴾ [and dense gardens] is the plural of ḥadīqah, which is an orchard, and al-ghulb are the large ones, thick of neck.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: al-ghulb are those whose parts are intertwined with one another. It is said: rajul aghlab (a man with a thick neck) when he has a large neck, and the lion is called aghlab because its neck is solid and it does not turn except with its whole body.

Al-Ajjaj said:
"I kept twisting my back and my head on the day of parting,
until I became like the thick-necked one (al-aghlab)."

The plural of aghlab and ghalbā’ is ghulb, just as aḥmar and ḥamrā’ are pluralized as ḥumr.

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: al-ghulb are the noble palm trees.

It is also reported from Ibn Zayd and ʿIkrimah: they are thick at the middle and the trunks.

Al-fākihah is what a person eats of the fruits of trees, such as grapes, figs, peaches and the like.

Al-abb is everything the earth produces that people do not eat and do not cultivate, of herbage and all kinds of pasture. The poet's verse includes it:
"Our grandfather is Qays, and Najd is our home,
and for us there is al-abb therein, and the watering place."

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: al-abb is everything that grows on the face of the earth.

Ibn Abi Talhah said: it is the fresh fruits.

It is also reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he said: it is specifically figs, but the first (view) is more preferable.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to explain the conditions of the return (to Allah), saying: ﴿فَإذا جاءَتِ الصّاخَّةُ﴾ [So when the Deafening Blast comes], meaning the Blast of the Day of Resurrection. It is called al-ṣākhkhah because of the intensity of its sound, for it deafens the ears, that is, it makes them deaf so that they do not hear. It has been said that it is called ṣākhkhah because ears incline toward it, from the saying aṣāḫa ilā kadhā, meaning "he listened to it." The first is more correct.

Al-Khalil said: al-ṣākhkhah is a cry that deafens the ears until it renders them deaf through the severity of its impact. The root of the word in the language is derived from a violent striking; it is said ṣakhkhahu bil-ḥajar when he struck him with a stone.

The answer to (idhā) is omitted, indicated by His statement ﴿لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنهم يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ﴾ [for every man among them that day will have a matter that occupies him], meaning: when the Deafening Blast comes, each person will be preoccupied with himself.

The time expression in His statement ﴿يَوْمَ يَفِرُّ المَرْءُ مِن أخِيهِ﴾ [on the day a man flees from his brother] ﴿وأُمِّهِ وأبِيهِ﴾ [and his mother and his father] ﴿وصاحِبَتِهِ وبَنِيهِ﴾ [and his spouse and his children] is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿إذا جاءَتْ﴾ [when it comes], or is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning "I mean," and it serves as an explanation of al-ṣākhkhah, or it is a substitute for it and is indeclinable, built on fatḥah. He specified these people for mention because they are the closest of relatives, and their children are (the objects of) tenderness and compassion. So fleeing from them occurs only due to a great terror and a dreadful calamity.

﴿لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنهم يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ﴾: that is, every person on the Day of Resurrection has a matter that preoccupies him away from his relatives and turns him away from them.

It has been said that he flees from them out of fear of their demanding from him what is owed between them. It has been said that he flees from them so that they do not see what he is in of hardship. It has been said that it is because he knows they will not benefit him nor avail him anything, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُغْنِي مَوْلًى عَنْ مَوْلًى شَيْئًا﴾ [the day when no protecting friend will avail a protecting friend at all]. The sentence is resumptive (mustanafah), brought to explain the cause of the fleeing.

Ibn Qutaybah said: yughnīhi means "it turns him away from his relatives," and from it one says aghniʿannī wajhaka, meaning "turn your face away from me."

The majority recited yughnīhi with the ghayn dotted (ghayn mu‘jamah).

Ibn Muḥaysin recited it with the unpointed ʿayn with the yāʾ vowelled with fatḥah, meaning yuhimmuhu: from ʿanāhu al-amr when it concerned him (ahammahu).

﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُسْفِرَةٌ﴾ [Faces that Day will be bright], "wujūh" is the subject (mubtada’), although it is indefinite, because it is in a context of detailing, and this is one of the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun. "Yawma'idhin" is related to it, and "musfirah" is its predicate (khabar). The meaning of musfirah is radiant and shining, and these are the faces of the believers, because they know on that day what blessings and honor are theirs. One says asfara al-ṣubḥ when it shone.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: musfirah (bright) from the traces of wuḍūʾ (ablution). It has been said: from the standing in prayer at night.

﴿ضاحِكَةٌ مُسْتَبْشِرَةٌ﴾ [laughing, joyful], meaning rejoicing at what they attained of the immense reward.

Then, when He finished mentioning the condition of the believers, He mentioned the condition of the disbelievers, saying: ﴿ووُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْها غَبَرَةٌ﴾ [And faces that Day will be dust-covered], meaning dust and gloom because of what they see of the punishment Allah has prepared for them.

﴿تَرْهَقُها قَتَرَةٌ﴾ [darkness will cover them], meaning blackness and dimness will cover and overspread them. It has been said: humiliation. It has been said: severity. In the speech of the Arabs al-qatar is dust, so said Abu ʿUbaydah, and he recited the verse of al-Farazdaq:
"Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a host
over whom you see banners and dust (al-qatara)."

What Abu ʿUbaydah said is refuted by the earlier mention of al-ghabarah, for it is the singular of dust (ghubār).

Zayd ibn Aslam said: al-qatarah is what rises up to the sky, and al-ghabarah is what descends to the earth.

﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ [Those], meaning the owners of these faces, ﴿هُمُ الكَفَرَةُ الفَجَرَةُ﴾ [they are the disbelievers, the wicked], meaning those who combine disbelief in Allah with wickedness. One says fajara, meaning he transgressed; and fajara, meaning he lied. Its root is inclination, and the fājir is one who inclines away from the truth.

At-Tirmidhi, who graded it ḥasan, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Ḥākim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, and Ibn Mardawayh, reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: "(The chapter) ʿAbasa wa tawallā was revealed concerning Ibn Umm Maktūm the blind man. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and began saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, guide me.' And with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was a man from the great leaders of the polytheists, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) began turning away from him and turning toward the other, saying: 'Do you see any harm in what I say?' He would say, 'No.' So concerning this it was revealed."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, and Abū Yaʿlā reported from Anas, who said: "ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm came while he (the Prophet) was speaking with Ubayy ibn Khalaf, so he turned away from him, and Allah revealed ﴿عَبَسَ وتَوَلّى﴾ [He frowned and turned away] ﴿أنْ جاءَهُ الأعْمى﴾ [because the blind man came to him]. So after that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to honor him."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was conversing privately with ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, al-ʿAbbās ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, and Abū Jahl ibn Hishām, and he was greatly eager to confront them and was keen that they should believe, a blind man named ʿAbdullāh ibn Umm Maktūm came toward them walking while he was speaking with them. ʿAbdullāh began asking the Prophet (ﷺ) to recite a verse of the Qur'an, saying: 'O Messenger of Allah, teach me from what Allah has taught you.' So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away from him, frowned in his face, turned away, disliked his speech, and turned toward the others. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished his private conversation and began to return to his family, Allah took away part of his sight, then he nodded his head, and then Allah revealed ﴿عَبَسَ وتَوَلّى﴾ [He frowned and turned away], the verse. When what was revealed concerning him was revealed, the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) honored him, spoke to him, and said: 'What is your need? Do you want anything?' And when he went away from him, he would say: 'Do you have any need for anything?'" Ibn Kathīr said: "In it there is strangeness, and its chain has been criticized."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿بِأيْدِي سَفَرَةٍ﴾ [in the hands of scribes], that he said: "scribes."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from him regarding ﴿بِأيْدِي سَفَرَةٍ﴾ that he said: "They are, in Nabatean, the readers."

Ibn Jarīr also reported from him regarding ﴿كِرامٍ بَرَرَةٍ﴾ [noble and righteous], that he said: "The angels."

al-Bukhārī, Muslim and others reported from ʿĀʾishah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The one who recites the Qur'an and is proficient in it is with the noble, righteous scribes, and the one who recites it and finds it difficult has two rewards."

Ibn Jarīr reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿ثُمَّ السَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُ﴾ [then He made the way easy for him], that he said: "He means by that his coming out from his mother's womb; He made it easy for him."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn al-Zubayr regarding His statement ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرِ الإنْسانُ إلى طَعامِهِ﴾ [let man look at his food], that he said: "To its entrance and its exit."

Ibn Abi al-Dunya reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿فَلْيَنْظُرِ الإنْسانُ إلى طَعامِهِ﴾, that he said: "To his excrement."

Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him regarding ﴿أنّا صَبَبْنا الماءَ صَبًّا﴾ [that We poured down the water in torrents], that he said: "The rain." ﴿ثُمَّ شَقَقْنا الأرْضَ شَقًّا﴾: "From the vegetation."

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim also reported from him regarding His statement ﴿وقَضْبًا﴾ [and fresh fodder], that he said: "The faṣfaṣah, meaning the qatt." ﴿وحَدائِقَ غُلْبًا﴾ [and dense gardens], he said: "Tall." ﴿وفاكِهَةً وأبًّا﴾ [and fruit and pasture], he said: "The fresh fruits."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim also reported from him, saying: "The ḥadā'iq are every densely intertwined (place), al-ghulb are what is thick, and al-abb is what the earth produces of what the animals eat and people do not eat."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from him also regarding ﴿وحَدائِقَ غُلْبًا﴾, that he said: "A tree in Paradise under which one takes shade, which bears nothing."

Ibn Jarīr reported from him also, saying: "Al-abb: the herbage and the pasture."

Abū ʿUbayd in his Faḍā'il and ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from Ibrahim al-Taymi, who said: Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about al-abb, what is it? He said: "What sky would shade me and what earth would carry me if I say something in the Book of Allah that I do not know?"

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd reported from ʿAbdullāh ibn Yazīd that a man asked ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) about His statement ﴿وأبًّا﴾, and when he saw them saying (nothing), he turned toward them with the whip (al-durrah).

Ibn Saʿd, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, al-Bayhaqī in al-Shuʿab, and al-Khaṭīb reported from Anas that ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) recited on the pulpit ﴿فَأنْبَتْنا فِيها﴾ [So We caused to grow therein] ﴿حَبًّا وعِنَبًا﴾ [grain and grapes], up to His statement ﴿وأبًّا﴾ [and pasture]. He said: "All of this we have known, so what is the abb?" Then he threw down a staff that was in his hand and said: "By the life of Allah, this is artificial (al-takalluf). What harm is there if you do not know what the abb is? Follow what has been made clear to you from this Book and act upon it, and what you do not know, leave it to its Lord."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "Al-ṣākhkhah is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His statement, musfirah, that he said: "Radiant." And regarding His statement ﴿تَرْهَقُها قَتَرَةٌ﴾, he said: "Severity and humiliation cover them."

Ibn Abi Ḥātim reported from him regarding qatarah, he said: "The blackness of the face."

Surah 80 (ʿAbasa) is Meccan, according to all scholars.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "The surah of ʿAbasa was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾ means he contracted his face and turned away.

It is also read ʿabbasa with the doubled letter (tashdid).

﴿Because the blind man came to him﴾ is a maf'ul li-ajlihi (object of purpose): that is, "because the blind man came to him." The governing verb for it is either ʿabasa or tawalla, according to the disagreement between the Basrans and the Kufans over the question of tanazuʿ (competition between two verbs for one complement): which is preferred, giving effect to the first or to the second?

The exegetes have agreed that the occasion of revelation of the verse was: "Some nobles of Quraysh were with the Prophet ﷺ, and he had hoped for their conversion. Then ʿAbd Allah ibn Umm Maktum came, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ disliked that Ibn Umm Maktum should cut off his speech, so he turned away from him, and this was revealed." The explanation of this will come, God willing, at the end of the discussion.

﴿And what could make you know? Perhaps he would purify himself﴾: Glory be to Him turned to address His Prophet ﷺ, because direct address is more forceful in reproach. That is: what makes you aware of his state, so that you turn away from him? The clause ﴿perhaps he would purify himself﴾ is resumptive, to explain that he has a matter that is incompatible with turning away from him: that is, perhaps he would purify himself from sins through righteous deeds, due to what he learns from you. So the pronoun in "perhaps he" refers to the blind man. It has also been said that it refers to the disbeliever: that is, "And what could make you know that what you hoped for from those with whom you were occupied in speech, instead of the blind man, that they would purify themselves or be reminded?" The first is preferable.

The word of hope (tarajji) is in respect of the one addressed, to alert that turning away from him, while he is hoped to purify himself, is impermissible. The majority read ﴿Because the blind man came to him﴾ as a statement without interrogation, and its basis is what has preceded.

Al-Hasan read ʾan jaʾahu with the long vowel (madd) as an interrogative. On this reading it is connected to a deleted verb indicated by ﴿He frowned and turned away﴾, and the estimate is: "Did the blind man come to him, [that] he turned away and withdrew?" A parallel to this verse is His saying in Surat al-Anʿam: ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord in the morning and evening﴾ [al-Anʿam: 52]. Likewise His saying in Surat al-Kahf: ﴿And do not let your eyes pass beyond them, desiring the adornment of the worldly life﴾ [al-Kahf: 28].

His saying: ﴿or he would remember﴾ is conjoined to "he would purify himself," included with it under the ruling of hope: that is, or he would remember and be admonished by what he has learned of the admonitions, ﴿so the reminder would benefit him﴾, i.e., the admonition.

The majority read "fa-tanfaʿuhu" with the nominative (raf'), while ʿAsim, Ibn Abi Ishaq, ʿIsa, al-Sulami and Zirr ibn Hubaysh read it with the accusative (nasb), as an answer to the optative/hope (jawab al-tarajji).

﴿As for the one who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾: that is, he was possessed of wealth and affluence, or he considered himself independent of faith and of what you possess of knowledge.

﴿you attend to him﴾: that is, you listen to his speech. Tasaddi means listening.

The majority read tasaddā with a single t (taxfif), by dropping one of the two tāʾs for lightness, while Nafiʿ and Ibn Muhaysin read it with doubling (tashdid), by assimilation (idgham). In this there is further repulsion for him ﷺ from turning towards them and listening to their speech.

﴿And it is not upon you that he does not purify himself﴾: that is, what is it upon you if he does not become Muslim and is not guided? For there is upon you only the conveying (of the message), so do not concern yourself with the affair of such disbelievers. It is permissible that "mā" be negating: that is, there is no harm upon you that the one to whom you turned and attended does not purify himself, and the clause is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun of "tasaddā."

Then Glory be to Him increased in reproaching His Messenger ﷺ, and said: ﴿But as for the one who came to you running﴾: that is, he reached you while being hasty in coming to you, seeking from you that you guide him to good and admonish him with the admonitions of Allah.

The clause ﴿while he fears﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the subject of "running" by interpenetration (tadakhkhul), or from the subject of "came to you" by coordination (tarādif).

﴿So you are unmindful of him﴾: that is, you are occupied away from him and turn away from attending to him, and talhhī means occupation and heedlessness. It is said: "lahaytu ʿan al-amr alhā," meaning I was occupied away from the matter; similarly "talahhaytu."

His saying: ﴿Nay [kallā]﴾ is a rebuke to him ﷺ concerning what he was reproached for: that is, do not do after this occurrence from you the like of it, of turning away from the poor and attending to the rich and being occupied with him, while he is not among those who purify themselves from receiving the guidance of what has come to you from the people of purification and acceptance of admonition. And this occurrence from the Prophet ﷺ is of the category of leaving the better course, so Allah, Glory be to Him, guided him to what is better for him.

﴿Indeed, it is a reminder﴾: that is, these verses or the surah are an admonition, whose due is that you be admonished by it, accept it, act upon its requirement, and that all your community act by it.

﴿So whoever wills, remembers it﴾: that is, whoever desires it is admonished by it, memorizes it and acts upon its requirement; and whoever turns away from it, as he did who considered himself self-sufficient, there is no need to concern oneself with his affair.

It has been said that the two pronouns in "innahā" and in "dhakarahu" refer to the Qur'an, and the feminine of the first is due to the feminine of its predicate.

It has been said that the first refers to the surah, or to the preceding verses.

The second refers to "tadhkirah" because it is in the sense of "dhikr."

It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿whoever wills, remembers it﴾ is: whoever Allah wills, He inspires and makes him understand the Qur'an until he remembers it and is admonished by it; but the first is preferable.

Then Glory be to Him informed of the greatness and majesty of this reminder, and said: ﴿in scrolls﴾: that is, it is a reminder existing in scrolls. So the prepositional phrase is an attribute of "tadhkirah," and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. "Ṣuḥuf" is the plural of ṣaḥīfah. The meaning of ﴿honored﴾ is that it is honored with Allah because of the knowledge and wisdom in it, or because it descends from the Preserved Tablet. It has been said that by "ṣuḥuf" is meant the books of the prophets, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scrolls, the scrolls of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-Aʿla: 18–19].

The meaning of ﴿exalted﴾ is that it is high in rank with Allah. It has been said: exalted in the seventh heaven.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: ﴿honored﴾, meaning the Preserved Tablet; ﴿exalted﴾, meaning in the seventh heaven.

Ibn Jarir said: exalted in rank and remembrance. It has also been said: exalted above resemblance and contradiction, purified, that is, sanctified, which none touch except the purified.

Al-Hasan said: purified from every defilement.

Al-Suddi said: protected from the disbelievers, who cannot reach it.

﴿In the hands of scribes﴾: "safarah" is the plural of "safir," like "katabah" and "katib." The meaning is that it is in the hands of scribes from among the angels, who copy the books from the Preserved Tablet.

Al-Farraʾ said: "The safarah here are the angels who carry the revelation between Allah and His Messenger, from al-sifārah, which is the mediation between people." He recited:

*"So I do not abandon mediation between my people, nor do I walk without a noble father."*

Al-Zajjaj said: The book was called "sifr" with a kasra on the sin, and the book is "sāfir," because its meaning is that it is clear. It is said: "asfara al-ṣubḥ" when it shines, and "asfarat al-mar'ah" when a woman uncovers her veil from her face; and from it: "safartu bayn al-qawm, usfiru sifārah," meaning I reconciled between them.

Mujahid said: they are the noble angels who record the deeds of the servants.

Qatadah said: the safarah here are the reciters, because they read the books.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: they are the companions of the Prophet ﷺ.

Then Glory be to Him praised the safarah, and said: ﴿noble, obedient﴾ [karam, barara]: that is, noble with their Lord; thus said al-Kalbi.

Al-Hasan said: noble from sins, for they raise themselves above them.

It has been said: they are too noble to be with the son of Adam when he is alone with his wife or relieves his need.

It has been said: they prefer the benefits of others over their own benefits.

It has been said: they show nobility toward the believers by seeking forgiveness for them.

"Barara" is the plural of bārr, like kafarah and kāfir: that is, pious, obedient to their Lord, truthful in their faith; and its explanation has already preceded.

﴿Killed is man, how disbelieving he is!﴾: that is, cursed is the disbelieving man, how severe is his disbelief. It has been said: "destroyed" (ʿudhdhiba) is meant. It has been said that by the man is meant ʿUtbah ibn Abi Lahab. The meaning of ﴿how disbelieving he is!﴾ is amazement at the excess of his disbelief.

Al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is, "Marvel, you, at his disbelief." It has been said that by "man" is meant the one previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿As for the one who thinks himself self-sufficient﴾. It has been said that it means the species, and this is the preferable view, so every intensely disbelieving disbeliever is included under it, and whoever was the cause of the revelation of the verse is included primarily.

Then Glory be to Him mentioned what this disbeliever should have considered, so that he might be restrained from his disbelief and refrain from his transgression. He said: ﴿From what thing did He create him?﴾: that is, from what thing did Allah create this disbeliever? The interrogative is for affirmation.

Then He explained that, saying: ﴿From a drop [nutfah] He created him﴾: that is, from a despised water, and this is belittling him.

Al-Hasan said: how can one who came out of the passage of urine twice be arrogant? The meaning of ﴿then He measured him﴾ is that He made him proportionate and prepared him for the interests of his self, and created for him the two hands, the two feet, the two eyes, and the rest of the instruments and senses. It has been said: He measured him in stages from one state to another: a drop, then a clot, until his creation was complete.

﴿Then the way He made easy for him﴾: that is, He made the path easy for him to good and evil.

Al-Suddi, Muqatil, ʿAta' and Qatadah said: He made it easy for him to come out from his mother's womb. The first is preferable.

Similar to it is His saying: ﴿And We guided him to the two paths﴾ [al-Balad: 10]. The accusative of "al-sabil" is by a hidden verb indicated by the mentioned verb: that is, He made the way easy, He made it easy for him.

﴿Then He causes him to die and buries him﴾: that is, He made him, after causing him to die, one having a grave in which he is concealed, honoring him, and did not make him one of those thrown upon the face of the earth to be eaten by beasts and birds. Thus said al-Farraʾ. Abu ʿUbaydah said: He made for him a grave and commanded that he be buried in it. He did not say "qabarahu," because the one who buries (qābir) is the one who interres with his own hand. From it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

*"If she had supported a dead man against her breast, he would have lived, and he would not have been moved to a gravedigger."*

﴿Then, when He wills, He will resurrect him﴾: that is, then when He wills his resurrection, He raises him, that is, revives him after his death. He tied the resurrection to His will to indicate that its time is not fixed, but follows His will. The majority read "anshara-hu" with an alif; Abu Haywah narrated from Nafiʿ and Shuʿayb ibn Abi Hamzah "nashara-hu" without an alif, and both are eloquent dialects.

﴿Nay! He has not fulfilled what He commanded him﴾: "Nay" is a rebuke and deterrence for the disbelieving man: that is, the matter is not as he says.

The meaning of "lammā yaqḍi mā amarahu" is: he has not fulfilled what Allah commanded him, of acting in obedience and avoiding His disobediences. It has been said that the intended meaning is mankind in general, and that he did not do what Allah commanded him despite the long duration, because no one is free of shortcoming.

Al-Hasan said: that is, truly he did not act upon what he was commanded.

Ibn Fawrak said: that is, "Nay, he has not fulfilled for this disbeliever what He commanded him of faith; rather He commanded him with what he did not fulfill."

Ibn al-Anbari said: stopping on "kallā" is ugly, and stopping on "amarahu" is good, and "kallā" by this is in the sense of "truly."

It has been said that the meaning is: not all individuals of mankind have fulfilled what He commanded, but some have neglected it: some through disbelief, and some through disobedience; and only a few have fulfilled what Allah commanded.

Then Glory be to Him began enumerating His blessings upon His servants so that they might be thankful and refrain from ingratitude, after mentioning the blessings connected with their coming into being. He said: ﴿So let man look at his food﴾: that is, let him look at how Allah created his food, which He made a cause of his life, and how He prepared for him the means of sustenance by which he prepares for eternal happiness. Mujahid said: its meaning is, "let man look at his food," that is, at its entry and its exit; but the first is preferable.

Then Glory be to Him explained that, saying: ﴿That We poured the water in torrents﴾. The majority read "innā" with a kasra, as a resumption. The Kufans and Ruways from Yaʿqub read it with a fatḥah, as a substitute (badal) from "his food," a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), since the descent of rain is a cause for the food's coming into being, so it is as though it includes it; or by estimating the lām of cause.

Al-Zajjaj said: the kasra is on the beginning and resumption, and the fatḥah is in the sense of a substitute from "food." The meaning: let man look at that We poured the water in torrents; and by pouring the water he meant the rain.

Al-Hasan ibn ʿAli read it with a fatḥah and imālah.

Then We split the earth, splitting it open [﴿ثُمَّ شَقَقْنا الأرْضَ شَقًّا﴾]: that is, We split it open with the vegetation that emerges from it due to the descent of rain, a wondrous splitting, with what comes forth from it in its smallness and greatness, its shape and its form.

Then He explained the cause of this splitting and what occurred for its sake, saying: ﴿فَأنْبَتْنا فِيها حَبًّا﴾ [So We caused grain to grow in it], meaning the grains on which one feeds. The meaning is that the plant continues to grow and increase until it becomes grain.

His statement ﴿وعِنَبًا﴾ [and grapes] is conjoined (ma'tuf) to ḥabban: that is, "and We caused grapes to grow in it." It has been said that it is not a requirement of conjunction that the conjoined element be restricted by all the restrictions that apply to the element it is conjoined to. So there is no harm in the growth of grapes being free of the splitting of the earth.

Al-qaḍb is the fresh fodder (qatt) that is cut again and again, and on which animals are fed. For this reason it is called qaḍb, as a verbal noun from qaḍaba-hu, meaning "he cut it," as if it is named for the repeated cutting of the same cut.

Al-Khalil said: al-qaḍb is fresh faṣfaṣa (alfalfa), and when it dries it becomes qatt.

In al-Ṣiḥāḥ it is said: al-qaḍbah and al-qaḍb are the fresh (plant), and he said: the place where it grows is called muqaḍḍabah.

Al-Qutaybi and Tha'lab said: The people of Makkah call grapes al-qaḍb.

Al-zaytun is that from which oil is pressed, and it is the well-known olive tree. Al-nakhl is the plural of nakhlah (palm tree).

﴿وحَدائِقَ غُلْبًا﴾ [and dense gardens] is the plural of ḥadīqah, which is an orchard, and al-ghulb are the large ones, thick of neck.

Qatadah and Muqatil said: al-ghulb are those whose parts are intertwined with one another. It is said: rajul aghlab (a man with a thick neck) when he has a large neck, and the lion is called aghlab because its neck is solid and it does not turn except with its whole body.

Al-Ajjaj said:
"I kept twisting my back and my head on the day of parting,
until I became like the thick-necked one (al-aghlab)."

The plural of aghlab and ghalbā’ is ghulb, just as aḥmar and ḥamrā’ are pluralized as ḥumr.

Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: al-ghulb are the noble palm trees.

It is also reported from Ibn Zayd and ʿIkrimah: they are thick at the middle and the trunks.

Al-fākihah is what a person eats of the fruits of trees, such as grapes, figs, peaches and the like.

Al-abb is everything the earth produces that people do not eat and do not cultivate, of herbage and all kinds of pasture. The poet's verse includes it:
"Our grandfather is Qays, and Najd is our home,
and for us there is al-abb therein, and the watering place."

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: al-abb is everything that grows on the face of the earth.

Ibn Abi Talhah said: it is the fresh fruits.

It is also reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk that he said: it is specifically figs, but the first (view) is more preferable.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to explain the conditions of the return (to Allah), saying: ﴿فَإذا جاءَتِ الصّاخَّةُ﴾ [So when the Deafening Blast comes], meaning the Blast of the Day of Resurrection. It is called al-ṣākhkhah because of the intensity of its sound, for it deafens the ears, that is, it makes them deaf so that they do not hear. It has been said that it is called ṣākhkhah because ears incline toward it, from the saying aṣāḫa ilā kadhā, meaning "he listened to it." The first is more correct.

Al-Khalil said: al-ṣākhkhah is a cry that deafens the ears until it renders them deaf through the severity of its impact. The root of the word in the language is derived from a violent striking; it is said ṣakhkhahu bil-ḥajar when he struck him with a stone.

The answer to (idhā) is omitted, indicated by His statement ﴿لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنهم يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ﴾ [for every man among them that day will have a matter that occupies him], meaning: when the Deafening Blast comes, each person will be preoccupied with himself.

The time expression in His statement ﴿يَوْمَ يَفِرُّ المَرْءُ مِن أخِيهِ﴾ [on the day a man flees from his brother] ﴿وأُمِّهِ وأبِيهِ﴾ [and his mother and his father] ﴿وصاحِبَتِهِ وبَنِيهِ﴾ [and his spouse and his children] is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿إذا جاءَتْ﴾ [when it comes], or is in the accusative governed by an implied verb, meaning "I mean," and it serves as an explanation of al-ṣākhkhah, or it is a substitute for it and is indeclinable, built on fatḥah. He specified these people for mention because they are the closest of relatives, and their children are (the objects of) tenderness and compassion. So fleeing from them occurs only due to a great terror and a dreadful calamity.

﴿لِكُلِّ امْرِئٍ مِنهم يَوْمَئِذٍ شَأْنٌ يُغْنِيهِ﴾: that is, every person on the Day of Resurrection has a matter that preoccupies him away from his relatives and turns him away from them.

It has been said that he flees from them out of fear of their demanding from him what is owed between them. It has been said that he flees from them so that they do not see what he is in of hardship. It has been said that it is because he knows they will not benefit him nor avail him anything, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿يَوْمَ لا يُغْنِي مَوْلًى عَنْ مَوْلًى شَيْئًا﴾ [the day when no protecting friend will avail a protecting friend at all]. The sentence is resumptive (mustanafah), brought to explain the cause of the fleeing.

Ibn Qutaybah said: yughnīhi means "it turns him away from his relatives," and from it one says aghniʿannī wajhaka, meaning "turn your face away from me."

The majority recited yughnīhi with the ghayn dotted (ghayn mu‘jamah).

Ibn Muḥaysin recited it with the unpointed ʿayn with the yāʾ vowelled with fatḥah, meaning yuhimmuhu: from ʿanāhu al-amr when it concerned him (ahammahu).

﴿وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ مُسْفِرَةٌ﴾ [Faces that Day will be bright], "wujūh" is the subject (mubtada’), although it is indefinite, because it is in a context of detailing, and this is one of the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun. "Yawma'idhin" is related to it, and "musfirah" is its predicate (khabar). The meaning of musfirah is radiant and shining, and these are the faces of the believers, because they know on that day what blessings and honor are theirs. One says asfara al-ṣubḥ when it shone.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: musfirah (bright) from the traces of wuḍūʾ (ablution). It has been said: from the standing in prayer at night.

﴿ضاحِكَةٌ مُسْتَبْشِرَةٌ﴾ [laughing, joyful], meaning rejoicing at what they attained of the immense reward.

Then, when He finished mentioning the condition of the believers, He mentioned the condition of the disbelievers, saying: ﴿ووُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ عَلَيْها غَبَرَةٌ﴾ [And faces that Day will be dust-covered], meaning dust and gloom because of what they see of the punishment Allah has prepared for them.

﴿تَرْهَقُها قَتَرَةٌ﴾ [darkness will cover them], meaning blackness and dimness will cover and overspread them. It has been said: humiliation. It has been said: severity. In the speech of the Arabs al-qatar is dust, so said Abu ʿUbaydah, and he recited the verse of al-Farazdaq:
